g-pos-09.reason: makes + object + adjective: 'makes the items far more accessible to the pickers'. access = noun, accessibly = adverb (nothing for it to modify; 'makes ... accessibly' is a flat-adverb error), accessibility = noun (items cannot equal 'accessibility').
g-pos-09.why: L pass (accessibility reads fine in 'far more accessibility to the pickers'); D pass ('makes' is ten words back); B fails (nobody actively believes accessibly/accessibility is right once 'makes the items' is seen) and S is a single step, so only medium.

g-pos-10.reason: The sentence needs a noun subject for 'will be accepted'. 'Applications for the ... position ... will be accepted'. Applying (gerund subject) cannot be 'accepted'; Applied (participle) leaves no subject; Apply is an imperative.
g-pos-10.why: L pass (Applying for the assistant branch manager position reads fine locally); D pass (the verb 'will be accepted' is after a relative clause); B fails (no good student actively believes 'Applying' as subject of 'will be accepted'), S weak, so floor-medium and close to easy in practice.
g-pos-10.editorNote: Very natural answer; consider making the participial distractor attractive (e.g. a verb whose -ing subject could be 'accepted').

g-tense-07.reason: 'when Ms. Ferrante was hired' is a past point; the centre had been operating before it (past perfect continuous). has been operating / is operating are blocked by 'was hired'; will have been is future.
g-tense-07.why: L, D pass (has been operating is fine in 'without any scheduling software for nearly two years'; the clue 'when ... was hired' is at the end). B is only partial: 'now handles' pushes toward present perfect, but 'when + past simple -> past perfect' is a textbook rule (cf. g-tense-06 precedent), and S is not needed. Borderline medium/hard.
g-tense-07.editorNote: Same design as g-tense-08 (non-restrictive which-clause pushing present perfect, past clue at the end).

g-tense-08.reason: 'last quarter' is a finished time, so simple past 'surpassed'. has surpassed cannot combine with 'last quarter'; had surpassed needs a later past reference; will surpass is future.
g-tense-08.why: L, D pass (has surpassed fits 'for the first time' locally; the decisive 'last quarter' is at the end). B is only partial: 'has grown since' and 'for the first time' prime present perfect, but 'last quarter + present perfect' is a well-known error; S not needed. Borderline medium/hard.
g-tense-08.editorNote: Pattern duplicates g-tense-07; a different tense pair would diversify the unit.

g-voice-04.reason: Reduced relative clause: 'The two interns [that] the head of the payroll department assigned to the benefits project last month have both been offered ...'. 'was/has been assigned' makes 'the head ... was assigned to the project' a complete clause, leaving 'The two interns ... have both been offered' hanging; the head cannot be assigned the interns' project anyway. assigning gives no finite verb.
g-voice-04.why: All four pass: L (was assigned reads as a full clause locally), D (the real main verb 'have both been offered' comes at the end), B (a complete clause feels right), S (must spot the contact/reduced relative and the interns as object of assigned).

g-participle-06.reason: The tenants received the notice, so the passive participle 'Given only two days' notice ..., the tenants ...'. Giving / Having given make the tenants the givers of notice of elevator repairs (illogical); To give is a purpose infinitive.
g-participle-06.why: L pass (Giving only two days' notice reads fine in the window); D pass (the subject 'the tenants' after the comma decides it). B fails: 'Given ...' is such a familiar opener that few good students believe the active forms; S minor.

g-participle-07.reason: 'Employees wishing to transfer ... should inform' - a participle phrase modifying Employees; the main verb is 'should inform'. wish and are wishing add a second finite verb; wished is a past/passive form that changes the meaning.
g-participle-07.why: L pass ('Employees wish to transfer to the new Corran Street office' is a fine clause locally); D pass (main verb 'should inform' is ~14 words later). B fails: 'Employees wishing to ...' is a stock formula good students recognise at once.

g-connect-07.reason: Before the comma there is only a noun phrase ('the revised safety regulations that the city council passed in March'; 'passed' belongs to the embedded relative clause), so a preposition is needed: 'In light of'. Because / Even though need a clause (Because of would be needed); Therefore is a conjunctive adverb.
g-connect-07.why: L pass (Because / Even though read as clauses because 'passed' looks like a verb); D pass (the missing finite verb is only evident at the comma, 14 words in); S pass (must notice 'passed' is inside a relative clause so no main verb precedes the comma). B partial.
g-connect-07.editorNote: Only one option is a preposition, so elimination by category helps test-takers; still a good trap.

g-connect-08.reason: 'Whether ... or not' = regardless of whether. 'If ... or not' as a clause-initial concessive is not standard formal English (if = whether only in indirect questions); Unless is logically wrong; Either needs 'or' without a clause and is the wrong word class.
g-connect-08.why: L pass (If the merger is approved by shareholders reads fine); D pass ('or not' comes 12 words later); B partial (if for whether is a common slip) but 'whether ... or not' is a very familiar pair, and S fails, so medium.
g-connect-08.editorNote: 'If ... or not' appears informally; an editor would change it, so legitimate trap.

g-agree-05.reason: The subject is 'The chief financial officer'; 'as well as the two external auditors ...' is parenthetical and does not make the subject plural, so 'is expected'. are / have been follow the plural 'auditors'; 'being' leaves no finite verb.
g-agree-05.why: All four pass: L (are expected fits the window), D (true subject is 13 words earlier), B (as well as treated like 'and' is a belief many good students hold), S (strip the as-well-as phrase and relative clause first).
g-agree-05.editorNote: Some usage sources tolerate plural agreement after 'as well as' with a plural nearest noun; formal editors prefer singular, so not flagged. Confidence 4 for that reason.

g-agree-06.reason: Subject is 'One' (of the vans), so singular 'has been'. 'have' is pulled by 'vans that deliver'. having / to have leave no finite verb.
g-agree-06.why: L pass (have been fits 'to our downtown branches ___ been'); D pass (subject 'One' is nine words back); S pass (must skip the relative clause and find the real subject). B partial: 'One of the + plural -> singular' is well known, so this sits at the low end of hard.
g-agree-06.editorNote: Not the contested 'one of the few X that is/are' type; plain 'One of the vans ... has' is unambiguous.

g-relative-05.reason: 'both of whom have advised' - relative pronoun, object of 'of', subject of the new clause. them creates a comma splice; who cannot follow a preposition; which is not used for people.
g-relative-05.why: L pass ('both of them have advised major retailers' reads fine locally); D pass (the earlier clause 'has hired ... consultants,' shows a relative is needed). B fails: 'both of whom' is a stock phrase good students know; S minor.

g-relative-06.reason: 'The hotel where the members ... stayed': where = at which. 'which' would need 'stayed at' (preposition missing); what and who are wrong for a place noun.
g-relative-06.why: L pass (The hotel which the members of our regional ... reads fine locally); D pass (the missing 'at' shows only at 'stayed during'). B fails: the answer is the form students choose on sight for a place noun, so the real trap is thin; S fails.
g-relative-06.editorNote: Naive 'place noun -> where' strategy gets it right; consider a version where the preposition-stranding reading ('which ... stayed at') is the tempting one.

g-pronoun-05.reason: 'familiarize themselves with' - the associates are both the agents and the ones to be familiarized (reflexive). 'them' would need a different referent that the sentence does not supply; 'their own' and 'they' are ungrammatical here.
g-pronoun-05.why: L pass ('to familiarize them with the return policy' reads fine locally); D pass (the antecedent 'the sales associates' is ten words back). B fails and S is minimal: 'familiarize oneself with' is a fixed collocation, so this is the lowest kind of medium.

g-pronoun-06.reason: 'so it signed a lease on a third' shows neither building was suitable: 'but neither had enough parking'. both / each / either all state or imply that the buildings did have parking, contradicting the lease on a third (and 'but either had' is also odd).
g-pronoun-06.why: L pass (but both/each had enough parking reads fine in the window); D pass (the decisive 'so it signed a lease on a third' is at the end). B fails: 'but' already points to a negative, so 'neither' is the natural choice; S fails.

g-prep-08.reason: blame A on B (blame the delay on the late arrival). 'for' would mean blaming the delay itself for the late arrival of beams (roles reversed and absurd: the delay in completion cannot cause late supplier deliveries); to / with are not used with blame.
g-prep-08.why: All four pass: L (chiefly for the late arrival reads fine), D ('blamed' is ten words before the gap), B (blame ... for is the form good students know), S (the object type, an effect not a person, decides blame on vs blame for).
g-prep-08.editorNote: 'for' is grammatical but semantically reversed, so a legitimate trap, not an alternative answer.

g-prep-09.reason: prevent + object + from + Ving. by / for / with do not follow prevent in this pattern ('prevents employees ... opening' without from is non-standard in American usage and is not offered).
g-prep-09.why: L pass ('training for/by opening files' reads fine locally); D pass ('prevents' is twelve words before the gap). B fails (prevent ... from is a drilled collocation) and S is only distance, so floor-medium; very familiar item type.
g-prep-09.editorNote: Near-formulaic; a distractor such as 'against' or 'of' would not add difficulty, but a verb with two real patterns would.

g-toing-05.reason: consider + Ving: 'is considering ... closing the branch office'. 'to close' is not used after consider; close / closed are not valid after the verb.
g-toing-05.why: L pass ('to close the branch office when its lease expires' reads fine, and 'To cut costs' primes a purpose reading); D pass ('considering' is eleven words before the gap). B is weak (consider + Ving is basic) and S is only one step (skip the inserted phrase), so medium.

g-toing-06.reason: 'closer ... to signing': 'to' is a preposition after (be) close, so Ving. 'to sign' is not used after close; 'for signing' and bare 'signing' are wrong prepositions/structures.
g-toing-06.why: All four pass: L (to sign a long-term agreement reads fine), D (closer is separated by a 14-word than-clause), B (to V is the form many good students believe), S (must first recognise 'to' as a preposition).

g-mandative-04.reason: 'requires ... that any shipment ... be invoiced': subjunctive/bare infinitive after require. 'being' and 'to be' are not finite; 'will be invoiced' is a future indicative that most editors would still change after 'requires that', though contract-style writing sometimes tolerates it.
g-mandative-04.why: All four pass: L (will be invoiced reads fine at the gap), D ('requires ... that' is far away), B (will be is the natural-feeling form), S (must find the that-clause across the inserted 'in the clause on late deliveries').
g-mandative-04.fix: Make the indicative clearly out: use a stronger mandative main verb (demands) or add wording that rules out a plain future 'will be invoiced' reading.
g-mandative-04.editorNote: 'requires that X will be Y' is not standard mandative usage but British indicative mandatives (4.3) make it borderline; shouldFix.

g-conditional-04.reason: Inverted second conditional 'Were the board ... to approve ...'. If / Unless cannot be followed by 'the board ... to approve' (no finite verb); Should + subject needs a bare infinitive ('Should the board approve'), not 'to approve'.
g-conditional-04.why: All four pass: L (If the board / Should the board read fine), D (the deciding 'to approve' is after a 12-word relative clause), B (Should + subject is a well-liked inversion), S (must skip the which-clause and see 'were ... to V').

g-compare-05.reason: 'more customers ... than': comparative with than. most / many / much do not take than in this way; much is also wrong with countable customers.
g-compare-05.why: L pass (serving many/most customers on an average weekday reads fine); D pass (than is five words after the gap). B fails and S fails: 'than' is a plain, common cue, so effectively the easy end of medium.

g-quantity-05.reason: 'The number of applicants ... has nearly doubled' - singular verb. 'A number of' means 'several' and takes a plural verb; 'The amount of' is for uncountables (editors change it to 'number'); 'A lot of applicants ... has' mismatches.
g-quantity-05.why: L pass (A number of / The amount of applicants read fine locally); D pass (the singular 'has' is nine words after 'applicants'); B pass (the number / a number mix-up is a classic false belief). S weak, but L+D+B suffice.
g-quantity-05.editorNote: 'The amount of applicants' is informal-only, so a legitimate trap.

g-parallel-04.reason: Parallel -ing list after 'include': ordering ..., scheduling ..., and managing .... to manage / manage / managed break the pattern.
g-parallel-04.why: L pass (and to manage the monthly budget reads fine in the window); D pass (the first two list items are ten words back). B fails and S fails: three -ing items in a row make this the easiest kind of medium, and the stem is formulaic.

shouldFix: g-mandative-04: 'will be invoiced' is a future indicative after 'requires that'; some contract-style and British indicative-mandative writing could let it through. Strengthen the stem so the indicative is clearly out (or swap in a distractor that is clearly not indicative).

batch: scene repetition. branch / new office / warehouse / store settings recur in about 10 of 24 items (pos-10, participle-07, relative-05, compare-05, parallel-04, toing-05, quantity-05, pos-09, pronoun-05, pronoun-06); vary the scenes (events, travel, HR, logistics, finance) per 1.4.
g-tense-07 / g-tense-08: same design twice (non-restrictive which-clause that primes present perfect, past-time clue at the end); change one to a different tense pair or clue type.
overall: Band counts: easy 0, medium 15, hard 9 (hard 37.5 percent, medium 62.5 percent, easy 0). Hard items: g-voice-04, g-connect-07, g-agree-05, g-agree-06, g-prep-08, g-toing-06, g-mandative-04, g-conditional-04, g-quantity-05. Hard meets the 30 percent target; medium is a little over the 45-55 percent band and there are no easy items, but no item fails the L test, so none can be judged easy under 3.4. Several mediums are low-grade (g-pos-10, g-prep-09, g-compare-05, g-parallel-04, g-pronoun-05) because the answer is a drilled collocation or a plain cue and B fails; these act as the batch's easy entries in practice (vsToeic easier). g-tense-07 and g-tense-08 are borderline medium/hard and were held at medium because the final-clause rules are textbook (same reasoning as g-tense-06). No item has a second defensible answer, so mustFix is empty. Compared with real TOEIC, the hard items (voice-04, conditional-04, toing-06, prep-08) are on par; the main gap is that the many 'noun phrase + long which-clause' stems repeat the same shape and the same branch/office scene, and a few medium items are too formulaic.
